But the church has its own firstfruits confession, the oldest words we possess: "Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures; and that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures" (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). That is our wandering-Aramean story, told over our own basket. We were perishing, we were in hard bondage to sin and death, we cried out, and a mighty hand brought us forth, not from Egypt this time but from the grave itself. And on the night He was betrayed, He put a basket in our hands to remember it by: "This do in remembrance of me" (Luke 22:19). Take the bread, and confess the story, every single time, lest the gift ever forget the grace that bought it.

Confess the story when you give.

## The Blessing and the Curse
*Standing between two mountains, and the curse is the longer list*

**Text:** Deuteronomy 27–28 · **Supporting:** Galatians 3:10–13 · Romans 3:19–20 · Daniel 9:11 · Deuteronomy 28:15

When Israel crossed into the land, Moses commanded a ceremony that would put the whole covenant on visible display in a single valley. Six tribes were to stand on Mount Gerizim to pronounce the blessing, and six on Mount Ebal to pronounce the curse, and the Levites would stand in the middle and read the law aloud while the whole nation answered "Amen" to every line (Deuteronomy 27:12–14). Blessing on one mountain, curse on the other, the people gathered in the valley between, forced to hear both and forced to assent to both with their own voices. This is covenant made visible, theater of the most serious kind, and you cannot stand in that valley and miss which of the two lists is longer.

**The blessing, and then the longer curse**
The blessing is real and it is generous and it is worth wanting. If Israel will faithfully obey, "Blessed shalt thou be in the city, and blessed shalt thou be in the field" (Deuteronomy 28:3). Blessed coming in and blessed going out, blessed in the fruit of the body and the fruit of the ground and the increase of the cattle, the barns full and overflowing, the nations defeated before them, the rain given in its season, lending to many and borrowing from none (Deuteronomy 28:4–12). Fourteen verses of blessing poured out on the people who keep covenant with their God. It is a beautiful and expansive list, and the nation said Amen to it.

And then Moses turns from Gerizim to Ebal, and the floor of the chapter drops out beneath you. "But it shall come to pass, if thou wilt not hearken unto the voice of the LORD thy God, to observe to do all his commandments... that all these curses shall come upon thee, and overtake thee" (Deuteronomy 28:15). And the curses run on for fifty-four relentless verses, nearly four times the length of the blessing. Cursed in the city and cursed in the field, the barns empty, wasting sickness, fever, drought, the sky like brass and the earth like iron, defeat before enemies, madness and blindness and confusion of heart, the harvest you planted eaten by another, your sons and daughters given to a people you do not know, and at the very bottom of the list, exile: "And the LORD shall scatter thee among all people, from the one end of the earth even unto the other" (Deuteronomy 28:64). The list descends so far into horror that it describes a besieged people driven to eat their own children. It is the most harrowing passage in the entire book, and Moses commands Israel to stand in the valley and say Amen to all of it.

**A warning the people will not finally keep**
The disproportionate length is the point, and the length is brutally honest. Moses is not balancing the ledger evenly, fifty-fifty, as though obedience and disobedience were equally likely outcomes for this people. He weights the curse far heavier on purpose, because he knows the people he is speaking to. He has already foreseen their failure aloud; he has called them stiffnecked to their faces; he will soon spell out their exile as a settled certainty. The disproportion between the blessing and the curse is itself a kind of prophecy. The curse is longer because the curse is coming. Centuries later, Daniel, praying in the rubble of Babylon with the exiles, would pray with this exact chapter open before him: "Yea, all Israel have transgressed thy law... therefore the curse is poured upon us, and the oath that is written in the law of Moses the servant of God, because we have sinned against him" (Daniel 9:11). The exile Moses described from the valley happened, in precise detail, because the people could not keep the covenant they stood and swore to keep.

This is the great crisis the law creates and cannot itself solve. The covenant says, with perfect clarity: obey and live under the blessing, disobey and fall under the curse. And then it sets that standard before a stiffnecked people that has already proven, with a golden calf, that it cannot meet the standard. The blessing of Gerizim is available in theory and unreachable in practice. The longer curse of Ebal is not pessimism or exaggeration. It is sober realism about the human heart, written into the very liturgy of the nation's first day in its promised home.

**The curse outweighs what we can carry, and Someone carried it**
We feel the full weight of this chapter the instant we stop reading it as somebody else's ancient history and start reading it as our own verdict. The law sets the same two mountains before us, and in our honest moments we know perfectly well which one we are standing under. Paul says it without softening a syllable: "For as many as are of the works of the law are under the curse: for it is written, Cursed is every one that continueth not in all things which are written in the book of the law to do them" (Galatians 3:10). All things. Continue in all of them, without exception, all the time. Not most. Not most days. And the curse falls on every soul that breaks even one command even once. By the deeds of the law no flesh will be justified in His sight, "for by the law is the knowledge of sin" (Romans 3:20). The law's deepest work, in the end, is to drive us down off both mountains into the valley between them and make us say Amen to a curse we have genuinely earned and cannot possibly survive.

I cannot carry this curse, and neither can you. That is exactly the truth Mount Ebal was built to teach a whole nation in one terrible afternoon. And it is precisely there, with the curse in full view and our own names written on it, that the gospel speaks its hardest and its best word: "Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us: for it is written, Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree" (Galatians 3:13). He went to Ebal in our place. He stood under the full length of the longer list, took every Amen we ever owed, hung on a tree outside the city, and absorbed the entire curse into His own body, so that the blessing of Gerizim, blessed in the city and blessed in the field, blessed coming in and blessed going out, might somehow come to people who never once kept the covenant. The curse outweighs what we can carry. So He carried it for us.

The curse outweighs what we can carry.

## Circumcise the Heart
*The covenant we cannot keep, and the God who promises to change us*

**Text:** Deuteronomy 29–30 · **Supporting:** Romans 2:28–29 · Ezekiel 36:26–27 · Romans 10:6–9 · Deuteronomy 30:6

Moses gathers the whole nation one final time to cut the covenant, and in the same breath he tells them, to their faces, that they are going to break it. "Neither with you only do I make this covenant and this oath; but with him that standeth here with us this day before the LORD our God, and also with him that is not here with us this day" (Deuteronomy 29:14–15). With the generations not yet born. And then, knowing all of it, Moses goes on to foresee the failure, the idolatry, the wrath, the uprooting, the scattering among the nations. He swears them to a covenant that he plainly says they will not keep. The question that hangs over these two chapters is almost unbearable: how can a people who cannot keep the covenant ever be saved by it?

**The diagnosis: a heart that cannot do it**
Moses names the problem with surgical precision, and he locates it exactly where we least want it located. Back in chapter 10 he had commanded Israel to circumcise the foreskin of their own hearts, to cut away their stubbornness themselves. Here the sheer impossibility of that command becomes the whole crisis of the book. The people have eyes but do not truly see, and ears but do not truly hear, and Moses tells them why: "yet the LORD hath not given you an heart to perceive, and eyes to see, and ears to hear, unto this day" (Deuteronomy 29:4). The defect is internal. It is not a shortage of information, they have the law, they watched the signs and wonders in Egypt with their own eyes, they stood at the foot of the burning mountain. It is a shortage of capacity. The heart itself is wrong, and a wrong heart cannot simply will itself right. You cannot command a stone to become flesh and expect the stone to comply.

This is the dead end the entire book has been driving toward from the first chapter. Love God with all your heart, but the heart is hard. Circumcise your own heart, but the knife cannot turn and cut itself. Keep the covenant and live, but the keeper is the very thing that is broken. Moses has set before Israel a righteousness they genuinely cannot reach, not because the law is pitched too high but because the heart is sunk too low. And he is honest enough to say it out loud to a people standing on the very edge of the land, baskets ready, oaths already on their lips.

**The promise: God will do the cutting**
And then, into that absolute dead end, Moses speaks the single most hopeful sentence in the book. After the failure he foresees, after the curse and the exile and the scattering, there will be a return, and the return will not be powered by Israel finally, somehow, trying harder than they ever managed before. "And the LORD thy God will circumcise thine heart, and the heart of thy seed, to love the LORD thy God with all thine heart, and with all thy soul, that thou mayest live" (Deuteronomy 30:6). The LORD will circumcise. God Himself takes up the knife. The surgery Israel could never perform on its own heart, God promises to perform on them, and the result of the surgery is precisely the thing the law demanded from the very beginning: a heart that loves God with everything it has.

This is the gospel buried in the heart of the law. The command of Deuteronomy 6 becomes, here in chapter 30, the promise of God. Love God with all your heart, and now: God will give you the very heart that does. Ezekiel saw the same surgery centuries later and named the instrument that makes it possible: "A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh. And I will put my spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes" (Ezekiel 36:26–27). I will cause you to walk. Not I will command you to walk and then leave you to manage it on your own strength, I will cause it from the inside. And Moses insists this promise is not distant or impossibly hard to reach: "But the word is very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart, that thou mayest do it" (Deuteronomy 30:14). Near. In the mouth and in the heart. Within reach.

**God must change the heart Himself, and in Christ He did**
We need this word more than any other word in all of Deuteronomy, because the whole modern church is busy trying to circumcise its own heart and calling the effort discipleship. We tell people to love God more, to try harder, to be more committed and more disciplined, as though the problem were a failure of effort and not a failure of capacity. We preach the command of chapter 6 with great urgency and we skip clean over the promise of chapter 30, and so we wear people out demanding a softness and a love from hearts of stone that can produce neither. I have done it from a pulpit, laid the full weight of the law on hearts that needed a Surgeon, not a louder and more passionate command.

Paul takes Deuteronomy 30 and lays it directly over the gospel, almost word for word: "The word is nigh thee, even in thy mouth, and in thy heart: that is, the word of faith, which we preach; That if thou shalt confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus, and shalt believe in thine heart that God hath raised him from the dead, thou shalt be saved" (Romans 10:8–9). The near word, the word in the mouth and in the heart, turns out to be Christ Himself. And the true circumcision, Paul says, "is that of the heart, in the spirit, and not in the letter; whose praise is not of men, but of God" (Romans 2:29). The surgery Moses promised is the new birth, performed by God, accomplished by the Spirit, purchased by the cross. We cannot change our own hearts. That is not finally a counsel of despair. It is the doorway into grace, because the same God who commands the new heart is the God who, in His Son, gives it.

God must change the heart Himself.

## Be Strong, for Moses Will Not Cross
*Leadership handed on, the law written down, and a song to convict*

**Text:** Deuteronomy 31 · **Supporting:** Joshua 1:5–9 · John 16:33 · 2 Timothy 4:6–8 · Deuteronomy 31:8

Moses is one hundred and twenty years old, and he begins his final chapter of action with a plain, unflinching admission of his own limit. "And he said unto them, I am an hundred and twenty years old this day; I can no more go out and come in: also the LORD hath said unto me, Thou shalt not go over this Jordan" (Deuteronomy 31:2). The great prophet, the man who spoke with God face to face on the mountain, says it without dramatizing it and without bitterness: I am not crossing. My part of this ends here, at the riverbank. The work of God will go on, and it will go on without me, on the far side of a river I will never see the other bank of.

**Be strong, the courage is in the presence**
So Moses hands the work to Joshua, and he does it publicly, in front of the whole assembled nation, so there can be no confusion about the succession. "Be strong and of a good courage, fear not, nor be afraid of them: for the LORD thy God, he it is that doth go with thee; he will not fail thee, nor forsake thee" (Deuteronomy 31:6). And then, turning to Joshua directly in the sight of all Israel, the same charge: "Be strong and of a good courage" (Deuteronomy 31:7). Notice carefully where the courage is grounded. Not in Joshua's competence, not in the size or training of the army, not in a brilliant strategy for the conquest. The courage rests on exactly one fact and nothing else, "the LORD, he it is that doth go before thee; he will be with thee, he will not fail thee, neither forsake thee: fear not, neither be dismayed" (Deuteronomy 31:8). The presence of God is the entire ground of the courage. Remove it and there is nothing left to be brave about; keep it and there is nothing left to fear.

This is leadership exactly as Scripture understands it, a man does his appointed part faithfully and then lets go, because the work was never anchored in him in the first place. Moses has carried this nation on his back for forty years, and he knows the great temptation at the moment of handoff is to believe, quietly, that it all depends on the leader and will collapse without him. It does not. The leader dies at the river; God crosses with the people anyway. So Joshua's commission is not "be capable enough to carry this alone." It is "be strong, because He goes with you." And God Himself would repeat the very charge to Joshua personally after Moses died: "as I was with Moses, so I will be with thee: I will not fail thee, nor forsake thee... Only be thou strong and very courageous... for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest" (Joshua 1:5, 7, 9). The presence is the promise that makes the courage possible.

**The law written, the song given against them**
But there is a darker thread running through this chapter, and Moses does not hide it or soften it. God tells him plainly, before the handoff is even finished, what is coming: "this people will rise up, and go a whoring after the gods of the strangers of the land, whither they go to be among them, and will forsake me, and break my covenant which I have made with them" (Deuteronomy 31:16). The succession happens under no illusion whatsoever. Even as Moses commissions Joshua and the people prepare to cross into the promise, God announces that the failure is certain. They will turn aside. It is not a risk to be managed; it is a future He already sees.

So Moses does two things to outlast the turning he knows is coming. First, he writes the law down and delivers it to the priests, commanding that it be read aloud to all Israel every seventh year and placed beside the ark of the covenant as a permanent witness (Deuteronomy 31:9, 24–26). Second, he is given a song to write and teach to the people, a song designed to function as a witness against them when they fall. "For when I shall have brought them into the land... and they shall have eaten and filled themselves, and waxen fat; then will they turn unto other gods... then shall this song testify against them as a witness; for it shall not be forgotten" (Deuteronomy 31:20–21). God writes the indictment before the crime is committed. He hands the people the words of their own conviction in advance, because He knows the heart that He has not yet changed. The written law beside the ark and the taught song in their mouths are mercies with teeth, they will not let Israel pretend, when the day of turning finally comes, that they were never warned.

**He knew we would turn aside**
This is the sober truth we genuinely need, and it cuts hard against everything sentimental in our religion. God does not enter into covenant with us on the cheerful assumption that we will rise nobly to meet it. He knows we will turn aside. He said it of Israel before they had set a single foot in the land, and He could say the very same thing of every one of us before we set a foot in the Christian life. There is no version of this story in which God was caught off guard by our faithlessness, surprised by our drift, blindsided by our sin. He knew. He wrote the song first.

I find that more comforting, in the end, than terrifying, because the only alternative is a God whose grace toward me depends on my reliability toward Him, and that is no grace at all. I have turned aside more times than I can count, and I have done it with my eyes open, knowing better, with the law beside the ark and the song already in my mouth. The handoff at the Jordan points past Joshua to the true and greater Joshua, Jesus, whose name is the very same name, the Leader who does cross the river ahead of His people, who does not die at the boundary and stop, but who breaks clean through it, and who said, with full and clear knowledge of every way His people would turn aside, "In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world" (John 16:33). Moses finished his course and handed it on. Paul, at his own death, would echo Moses' very posture: "I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith" (2 Timothy 4:7). The work outlasts the worker, every time, because the One who goes before the people does not fail and will not forsake, even a people He knew, from the beginning, would turn aside.

He knew we would turn aside.

## The Song of Moses
*A faithful Rock, a faithless people, and atonement at the end*

**Text:** Deuteronomy 32 · **Supporting:** Romans 10:19 · Romans 12:19 · 1 Corinthians 10:4 · Deuteronomy 32:4

When God told Moses the people would turn aside, He gave Moses a song to write and teach them, and now, in this chapter, Moses stands and sings it in the ears of the whole congregation. It is the longest poem in the Torah, and it has one governing architecture from beginning to end: a faithful God set in stark relief against a faithless people, line after relentless line, until the contrast is total and inescapable. "He is the Rock, his work is perfect: for all his ways are judgment: a God of truth and without iniquity, just and right is he" (Deuteronomy 32:4). The Rock. Perfect in His work, true, without a trace of iniquity, just and right in all His ways. That is the first note of the song, and every other line in it is measured against that opening chord.

**The Rock who found Jacob in the desert**
The song tells Israel's story as a love song that curdled into betrayal. God found Jacob "in a desert land, and in the waste howling wilderness; he led him about, he instructed him, he kept him as the apple of his eye" (Deuteronomy 32:10). The apple of His eye, the pupil, the most tender and most fiercely guarded thing the whole body owns. That is the most affectionate phrase in all of Deuteronomy. God did not find Israel as a great and accomplished nation and recruit them for their strength. He found them as nothing, as nobody, in a howling wasteland, and He cherished them like the very pupil of His own eye. He carried them the way an eagle teaches its young to fly: "As an eagle stirreth up her nest, fluttereth over her young, spreadeth abroad her wings, taketh them, beareth them on her wings" (Deuteronomy 32:11). Pure, unearned, fierce, protective tenderness, lavished on a people who brought nothing to it.

And then the turn the whole song exists to expose. "But Jeshurun waxed fat, and kicked: thou art waxen fat, thou art grown thick, thou art covered with fatness; then he forsook God which made him, and lightly esteemed the Rock of his salvation" (Deuteronomy 32:15). Fed to fullness, and then kicking the One who fed him. It is the exact warning of chapter 8, now set to music and aimed at the heart. "Of the Rock that begat thee thou art unmindful, and hast forgotten God that formed thee" (Deuteronomy 32:18). They sacrificed to demons, to new gods that came newly up, gods their fathers had never feared or known (Deuteronomy 32:17). The people fed and carried on the eagle's wings kicked the very wings that bore them up. The faithlessness is not an incidental detail in this song, it is the whole indictment, set to a melody on purpose, so that Israel would have to hear their own betrayal coming out of their own mouths when the predicted day finally arrived. God would later use even their faithlessness, Paul notes, to provoke them, "I will provoke you to jealousy by them that are no people" (Romans 10:19).

**Vengeance, and then atonement**
The song moves on toward judgment, and the anger of God in it is real and named without flinching: "For a fire is kindled in mine anger, and shall burn unto the lowest hell, and shall consume the earth with her increase" (Deuteronomy 32:22). "To me belongeth vengeance, and recompence; their foot shall slide in due time" (Deuteronomy 32:35), the very line Paul would later quote to forbid the church its own revenge: "Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord" (Romans 12:19). The faithless people have earned the fire, and the song does not pretend otherwise or soften the verdict to make it easier to sing.

But, and this is everything, the song does not end in fire. It ends in mercy, and the mercy is genuinely stunning given everything that has come before it. God says He will not finally hand His people over to the enemy to be utterly destroyed, because the enemy would then boast that their own hand had triumphed and would dangerously misread the judgment as their own strength (Deuteronomy 32:27). And then the closing note of the whole song: "Rejoice, O ye nations, with his people: for he will avenge the blood of his servants... and will be merciful unto his land, and to his people" (Deuteronomy 32:43). He atones. The song that opened with a perfect Rock and a kicking, fat, forgetful people closes with that same Rock making atonement for the land and for the very people who forsook Him. The faithfulness of God outlasts and overpowers the faithlessness of the people. That, and nothing else, is the only reason the song does not end in ash and silence.

**The Rock is faithful. We are not.**
This is the song the church needs to keep singing, because it tells the unvarnished truth about both parties in the covenant and lets neither one off the hook. We are Jeshurun. We waxed fat and we kicked. We were found in a wasteland and carried on eagle's wings and kept as the apple of His eye, and we have lightly esteemed the Rock of our salvation more times than we could ever number, fed by His grace and forsaking His wings in the very same breath. I am unmindful of the Rock that begat me on a weekly, sometimes daily, basis. This song is not the record of one ancient people's failure, safely behind us. It is the honest autobiography of every believer who was loved up out of the waste and then forgot it in the plenty.

And the Rock in this song has a name the New Testament will not let us miss or spiritualize away. Paul says that the people in the wilderness "did all drink the same spiritual drink: for they drank of that spiritual Rock that followed them: and that Rock was Christ" (1 Corinthians 10:4). The Rock who found Jacob in the desert, who is perfect and true and without iniquity, who alone makes atonement for a faithless people, that Rock is Jesus. And the vengeance the song promised and the atonement the song promised meet at one single place in all of history: a cross, where the fire of God's just and kindled anger fell at last, not on the faithless people who had earned it, but on the faithful Rock who stepped into their place and took it. He is faithful. We are not. That is the whole gospel, set to music a thousand years before the cross was raised.

The Rock is faithful. We are not.

## The Blessing of Moses
*The man of God speaks grace over a flawed people on his way out*

**Text:** Deuteronomy 33 · **Supporting:** Genesis 49:28 · Hebrews 7:25 · Romans 8:34 · Deuteronomy 33:27

The last words a dying man chooses are the truest thing about him. Moses, the day before he climbs the mountain to die, does not curse the people who broke his heart for forty years, who grumbled and rebelled and built a golden calf at the foot of the holy mountain, who tested God at the waters and provoked Moses until he sinned and was barred from the very land he is about to see and never enter. He does not settle scores. He blesses them. "And this is the blessing, wherewith Moses the man of God blessed the children of Israel before his death" (Deuteronomy 33:1). The man of God, the only place in all the Torah where Moses is given that particular title, uses his final breath to speak grace over a deeply flawed people, tribe by tribe, name by name.

**Grace spoken over each tribe by name**
Moses goes through the tribes one at a time, and the tenderness is remarkable precisely because of everything he knows about each of them. He blesses Reuben, the firstborn who forfeited his birthright in disgrace, asking simply that he "live, and not die" (Deuteronomy 33:6). He blesses Judah and prays that God would bring him in to his people and be a help against his enemies. He entrusts Levi with the priesthood and the holy things, the very tribe that had failed at the calf. He calls Benjamin "the beloved of the LORD" who "shall dwell in safety by him," and says of him that the LORD "shall dwell between his shoulders" (Deuteronomy 33:12), carried close, like a child borne on his father's back. And to Joseph he gives the richest blessing of all, "for the precious things of heaven, for the dew, and for the deep that coucheth beneath... and for the good will of him that dwelt in the bush" (Deuteronomy 33:13–16). Tribe by tribe, the dying prophet speaks not their long record of failures but their God-given futures.

This is exactly how Jacob, generations earlier, had left the world, gathering his sons to his deathbed and blessing them one by one before he died: "All these are the twelve tribes of Israel: and this is it that their father spake unto them, and blessed them; every one according to his blessing he blessed them" (Genesis 49:28). It is how the spiritual fathers of Israel left this life, not by tallying up the sins of their children and pronouncing a final verdict, but by speaking blessing over them, calling them forward toward what God Himself would yet make of them. Moses, the spiritual father of the whole nation, leaves the very same way. The man who carried this stubborn people across a wilderness, who threw himself between them and the consuming wrath when God offered to destroy them and start over, now blesses them by name at the very end, because love that has stayed through all the failure speaks grace, and not verdict, over the grave.

**There is none like the God of Jeshurun**
And right at the heart of the blessing, Moses lifts his eyes off the tribes and fixes them on their God, and the praise that comes out is the highest in the entire book. "There is none like unto the God of Jeshurun, who rideth upon the heaven in thy help, and in his excellency on the sky. The eternal God is thy refuge, and underneath are the everlasting arms" (Deuteronomy 33:26–27). There is none like Him. He rides across the very heavens to come to your aid. He is a refuge to flee into, and underneath you, beneath all the falling, beneath all the failing, beneath the whole accumulated weight of a flawed and faithless people, are the everlasting arms that have no bottom and no end.

That is the foundation the entire blessing rests on, and it is the only foundation that could hold it. Moses can speak genuine grace over a faithless nation because the God of that nation is unlike any other god there is, a God who rides the sky to reach His people, whose arms are underneath them even and especially when they fall. The blessing is not finally optimism about the tribes; Moses had no illusions about the tribes. It is confidence about their God. Israel's future is secure not because Israel is faithful but because underneath Israel, always and at the lowest point, are the everlasting arms that simply do not let go.

**He blessed them on his way out, and so does the better Mediator**
We need this picture of how love finishes its course, because we are so strongly tempted to leave people, and to leave this life, holding our careful accounts of their failures rather than speaking blessing over their futures. We total up the wrongs done to us. We rehearse the disappointments one more time. And then we die, and we lead, and we parent, gripping the ledger instead of opening our hands to speak the blessing. Moses had more reason than any of us to keep the ledger open, these people cost him the promised land itself, and he tore the ledger up and blessed them by name on his way to his own grave.

I am convicted by how rarely I leave a room, or a relationship, or a hard and painful season, the way Moses left the entire world, with real grace on my lips for the very people who wounded me deepest. But Moses points past himself, as he always does, to the One whose whole ongoing ministry is to bless His failing people from the place we ourselves cannot yet follow. Moses blessed Israel and then climbed Mount Nebo alone to die outside the land. Jesus blessed His own, "he lifted up his hands, and blessed them. And it came to pass, while he blessed them, he was parted from them, and carried up into heaven" (Luke 24:50–51), and He went not to a lonely grave outside the land but to a throne, where "he ever liveth to make intercession" for those who come to God by Him (Hebrews 7:25). The man of God blessed them on his way out. The Son of God blesses us still, from the inside of heaven, where He "is even at the right hand of God, who also maketh intercession for us" (Romans 8:34). And underneath us, beneath our every failure, are the everlasting arms.

He blessed them on his way out.

## The Death of Moses
*He saw the whole land, and died outside it*

**Text:** Deuteronomy 34 · **Supporting:** Hebrews 11:13 · Matthew 17:1–4 · Hebrews 4:8–9 · Deuteronomy 34:10

The book of the law ends with a funeral. Moses climbs to the top of Mount Nebo, to the peak of Pisgah across from Jericho, and the LORD shows him the whole land spread out beneath him, Gilead as far as Dan, all of Naphtali, the land of Ephraim and Manasseh, all the land of Judah out to the western sea, the Negev, the plain, the valley of Jericho the city of palm trees, as far as Zoar. "And the LORD said unto him, This is the land which I sware unto Abraham, unto Isaac, and unto Jacob, saying, I will give it unto thy seed: I have caused thee to see it with thine eyes, but thou shalt not go over thither" (Deuteronomy 34:4). He sees all of it. Every hill of the ancient promise laid out at his feet. And then the very next verse: "So Moses the servant of the LORD died there in the land of Moab, according to the word of the LORD" (Deuteronomy 34:5). He saw the land, and he died outside of it.

**The grave God dug**
The detail that follows is one of the strangest tendernesses in all of Scripture. "And he buried him in a valley in the land of Moab, over against Bethpeor: but no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day" (Deuteronomy 34:6). God buried Moses. With no human hand to dig the grave or lay the body, in a place no one would ever find or mark, the LORD Himself laid His servant down in the ground. There would be no shrine built over it, no annual pilgrimage to it, no tomb to be venerated or fought over by later generations. The greatest prophet Israel ever produced has an unmarked grave in a foreign valley, dug by the hand of God alone.

And the text is careful to tell us he did not die of weakness or decline: "Moses was an hundred and twenty years old when he died: his eye was not dim, nor his natural force abated" (Deuteronomy 34:7). His sight was clear. His strength was unbroken. He did not fade out. He died at the word of God, strong to the very end, kept out of the land for one act of unbelief at the waters of Meribah, where he had struck the rock in anger and seized for himself a sliver of the glory that belonged to God alone. There is a sobering lesson buried in that grave: the law cannot bring even its own mediator across the river. The man who delivered the entire covenant to Israel could not himself be carried into the promise by it. He saw it, and he died, and God buried him in the dark.

**The one who lived by faith and did not receive the promise**
This is the deepest note in the chapter, and the book of Hebrews would later take it and make it the very pattern of all faith. The great heroes of faith "all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth" (Hebrews 11:13). Seen them afar off. That is Moses on Nebo, precisely, seeing the promise spread out plainly with his own undimmed eyes, and dying before he could ever walk a single step into it, trusting a God who keeps His sworn word out beyond the edge of one man's single life. The land Moses could not enter was real, and God did give it; Moses simply did not live to set his foot on it. Faith is sometimes exactly this: seeing the promise from the mountain and dying outside of it, certain it will be kept anyway, by Someone else, for someone else.

And the book of the law closes on an aching, unresolved admission. "And there arose not a prophet since in Israel like unto Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face" (Deuteronomy 34:10). Like unto Moses, the very phrase from chapter 18, the Prophet like Moses who was promised to come. And the final verse of the whole book quietly confesses: he has not come yet. The seat is still empty. The promise of a greater prophet hangs over the closing funeral, unfulfilled and unanswered. Deuteronomy ends with a grave in Moab and an open question left hanging in the air. Where is the Prophet like Moses?

**He saw the land and died outside, until One came who could enter it**
We stand where Moses stood on that mountain far more often than we like to admit, shown the promise, persuaded of it, and dying outside of it. We bury people who saw the land clearly and never once entered it. We carry hopes that God has sworn to and will plainly not see fulfilled within our own short years. And the constant temptation is to read the unmarked grave on Nebo as defeat, as the law's final failure, as a story that simply runs out and ends in the dark of a foreign valley. But it does not end there, and it was never meant to.

Because the Prophet like Moses did come at last, and Hebrews tells us precisely why Moses himself had to wait outside the land: "For if Jesus had given them rest, then would he not afterward have spoken of another day. There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God" (Hebrews 4:8–9). Joshua brought the next generation into the land, but he could not bring them into the true rest; that rest was reserved and waiting for the true and greater Joshua, whose name is the same name. And the most beautiful answer of all comes centuries later, on another mountain entirely, where the man who died outside the land is finally seen standing inside it. On the Mount of Transfiguration, when Jesus was transfigured in glory before His disciples, "behold, there appeared unto them Moses and Elias talking with him" (Matthew 17:3). Moses, in the promised land at last, not brought in by the law that had kept him out, but standing there in conversation beside the Prophet like Moses whom God had finally raised up and sent. The grave that God dug in Moab did not hold him in the end. He saw the land and he died outside it. And then he stood inside it, with Christ, the One who brings all His people across the very river that the law never could.

He saw the land and died outside.
